summary: A sedating older (first-generation) antipsychotic used in Canada for psychosis, acute mania, severe anxiety, and short-term insomnia. It is strongly calming, but compared with newer antipsychotics it carries a higher risk of low blood pressure, drying side effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision), and movement side effects.
description: Methotrimeprazine (also called levomepromazine) is a very sedating older antipsychotic used in Canada for schizophrenia/psychosis and bipolar disorder, and sometimes for severe anxiety or short-term insomnia when sedation is actually the goal. It can calm agitation quickly, but it can also drop blood pressure and cause heavy daytime sleepiness, dry mouth, constipation, and movement side effects: stiffness, shaking or restlessness, and tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements, often of the face or mouth, that can last). It is not available in the U.S. It should not be used at all if you have liver disease.
patient_summary: This is a “knock-the-volume-down” antipsychotic. People often feel calmer and sleepier—sometimes too sleepy. It can help with agitation, racing thoughts, and insomnia, but it can also cause dizziness when standing, dry mouth/constipation, and movement side effects. It’s not a casual med, and it’s not a long-term sleep fix.

primary.context: Used for schizophrenia/psychosis when an antipsychotic is needed and strong sedation may be helpful (for example, severe agitation or insomnia tied to psychosis).
Used in bipolar disorder and acute mania. Calming effects can show up within days, with fuller mood stabilization over 1 to 2 weeks.

off_label.context: In practice, it’s sometimes used short-term for severe anxiety when sedation is a benefit. Tablet labeling in Canada includes anxiety-related conditions.
Sometimes used as a short-term sleep agent (especially when insomnia is driven by agitation, mania, or psychosis). Not a long-term insomnia strategy.

therapeutic_response.display: IM for anxiety/tension: ~1 hour; oral effects for mania may be noticed within days; oral effects for schizophrenia may be noticed within 1-2 weeks

common_adverse_effects.notes: This is a sedating antipsychotic. Many people feel sleepy, slowed, or “heavy,” especially early on or after dose increases. If daytime sedation is too much, clinicians often shift more dosing to bedtime and keep daytime doses smaller.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dizziness or faintness when standing up (a drop in blood pressure)
common_adverse_effects.notes: This can happen even at therapeutic doses and is more likely with injections and higher doses. Get up slowly, hydrate, and let your prescriber know if you’re having near-fainting episodes.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dry mouth, constipation, trouble peeing, blurry vision (anticholinergic effects)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Dry mouth and constipation are common with phenothiazines. Constipation can become severe—don’t ignore it. Urinary retention or severe belly pain needs urgent evaluation.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Stiffness, shaking or restlessness (movement side effects, EPS)
common_adverse_effects.notes: EPS can look like inner restlessness (akathisia), stiffness, tremor, slowed movement, or muscle spasms. Tell your prescriber quickly—early management matters.
Glucose intolerance and hyperglycemia have been reported with antipsychotics. If you have diabetes or are at risk, monitoring matters.
Antipsychotics can raise the hormone prolactin. Signs can include period changes, low sex drive, erection or ejaculation changes, breast tenderness, or milky discharge from the nipple.

serious_risks.risk: A rare emergency (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS): fever, severe muscle stiffness, confusion, and unstable blood pressure, heart rate or sweating. This is a medical emergency.

Serious heart-rhythm problems, including QT prolongation (a heart-rhythm change seen on an ECG) and torsades de pointes (a dangerous heart rhythm): fainting, pounding heartbeat, sudden collapse. This is a medical emergency.
Very low blood pressure or circulatory collapse (especially with injections): fainting, shock. This is a medical emergency.
A dangerous drop in white blood cells (agranulocytosis or neutropenia — infection risk): fever, sore throat, infections. Get checked urgently.
Tardive dyskinesia (TD): involuntary movements (often of the face or tongue) that can last; the risk goes up with long-term use.
Seizures: phenothiazines can lower seizure threshold.
Paralytic ileus/necrotizing enterocolitis (rare but severe GI complications): severe abdominal pain/distention, vomiting, no stool/gas. EMERGENCY.
Severe hypersensitivity reactions: angioedema, Stevens-Johnson syndrome. EMERGENCY.

safety.black_box_warning: Canadian boxed warning: Older adults with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death compared with placebo. Methotrimeprazine is not indicated for dementia-related psychosis in elderly patients.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to methotrimeprazine/phenothiazines or any component
Coma or significant CNS depression due to alcohol, hypnotics, analgesics, or opioids

For the injection only: low blood cell production in the bone marrow, very low blood pressure or circulatory collapse, severe heart disorders, myasthenia gravis, pheochromocytoma, regional/spinal anesthesia, risk of closed-angle glaucoma or trouble peeing from prostate or urethra problems, a past dangerous drop in white blood cells (agranulocytosis), taking other antipsychotics or dopamine medicines at the same time, and babies under 1 year (injection restrictions vary by product)

precautions: It should not be used if you have liver disease.
QT prolongation and life-threatening arrhythmias have been reported with phenothiazines; risk rises with electrolyte problems and other QT-prolonging meds.
Dizziness or fainting when standing up (a drop in blood pressure) can be significant, especially after an injection or higher doses by mouth.
CNS depression: can impair driving, decision-making, coordination, and increase fall risk.
Stiffness, shaking or restlessness (movement side effects, EPS) and tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements that can last) can happen; the risk goes up with higher doses and longer use.
A rare but life-threatening reaction (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS) can cause fever, muscle rigidity, confusion, and unstable blood pressure, heart rate or sweating.
A dangerous drop in white blood cells (agranulocytosis) has been reported with antipsychotics, so take signs of infection seriously.
Drying (anticholinergic) effects can be strong: constipation, trouble peeing, blurry vision, dry mouth. A blocked, stopped-up bowel (paralytic ileus) is an emergency.
Trouble controlling body temperature: higher risk with heat, dehydration, hard exercise, and other medicines with drying (anticholinergic) effects.

interactions.mechanism: Additive CNS depression and impaired coordination; higher risk of respiratory depression, falls, and dangerous sedation.
interactions.action: Avoid. If you’re drinking, this is the wrong medication for you right now.

interactions.mechanism: Severe sleepiness, dangerously slow breathing, low blood pressure, and falls; the risk multiplies, not just adds.
interactions.action: Avoid or use only with tight coordination and monitoring. Start low, go slow.

interactions.interactant: Benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants, cannabis
interactions.mechanism: Excess sedation, confusion, impaired judgment, falls, and (in vulnerable people) delirium.
interactions.action: Minimize combinations whenever possible. If combined, use the lowest effective doses and monitor closely.

interactions.interactant: QT-prolonging medications (certain antidepressants, antibiotics, antiarrhythmics, methadone, etc.)
interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of QT prolongation (a heart-rhythm change seen on an ECG) and torsades de pointes (a dangerous heart rhythm), especially with low potassium or magnesium.
interactions.action: Review the full med list. Consider baseline ECG and electrolyte checks if risk factors exist.

interactions.interactant: Medicines with anticholinergic (drying) effects (benztropine, diphenhydramine, tricyclics, some bladder medicines)
interactions.mechanism: Worsened constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, dry mouth, confusion/delirium—especially in older adults.
interactions.action: Keep the total load of drying medicines as low as possible, and have a plan for constipation.

interactions.interactant: Dopamine agonists (e.g., Parkinson’s meds) and stimulants
interactions.mechanism: They work against each other, so one or both may work less well, and psychosis may get worse.
interactions.action: Coordinate carefully with neurology/psychiatry. Often best avoided or managed with a clear plan.

interactions.mechanism: Together they can lower blood pressure more and cause dizziness and falls.
interactions.action: Monitor blood pressure, especially early on and after dose increases.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that block or speed up the liver enzyme CYP3A4 (which helps break it down)
interactions.mechanism: Potential level changes (CYP3A4 is noted as a minor substrate pathway).
interactions.action: Still worth checking for major interaction flags if you’re on multiple meds.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Mental status and alertness every visit: sedation level, confusion, and whether daytime functioning is getting crushed.
Blood pressure and orthostatics, especially after starting, after dose increases, and after parenteral doses; watch for dizziness/falls.

Movement side effects at every visit: restlessness (akathisia), muscle spasms (dystonia), and Parkinson-like stiffness or shaking. A formal rating scale at least yearly, or every 6 months if risk is high.
Checks for tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements that can last) at every visit, with a formal scale at least yearly (more often if risk is high).
Fall risk assessment as clinically indicated; extra vigilance in older adults and those with prior falls.

Metabolic monitoring: weight/BMI frequently early (every visit for first months, then periodically), fasting glucose/HbA1c and lipids at baseline and periodically (e.g., around 4 months after initiation and annually, sooner if abnormal).
Blood counts (CBC) as needed, especially if you get signs of infection (fever, sore throat) or have had low white blood cells before, including from a medicine.
Blood salts and kidney function as needed; blood sodium in older adults, because of the risk of low blood sodium (hyponatremia), which can cause confusion, headache or seizures.
ECG when clinically indicated (history of QT issues, cardiac disease, syncope, multiple QT-prolonging meds, electrolyte risk).
Signs of high prolactin (a hormone): period changes, changes in sex drive, breast growth in men, milky nipple discharge, erection or ejaculation problems; a prolactin blood test if you have symptoms.
Constipation and urinary retention checks: treat constipation early; urgent evaluation for severe abdominal pain/distention or inability to urinate.
Body temperature: advice about heat, dehydration, and hard exercise, especially if you take other medicines with drying (anticholinergic) effects.
Ocular symptoms: assess vision changes; consider eye exam if prolonged exposure or symptoms arise.

special_populations.pregnancy: Data on methotrimeprazine itself are limited. As a group, older antipsychotics have not shown a clear rise in major birth defects overall, but use late in pregnancy can cause movement symptoms and/or withdrawal in newborns (agitation, abnormal muscle tone, tremor, feeding problems, breathing trouble, sleepiness). Tapering off late in pregnancy to prevent newborn symptoms is generally not recommended; instead, the lowest dose that works is used, avoiding multiple medicines when possible. For anxiety in pregnancy, other options are usually preferred.
special_populations.lactation: Present in human milk; the manufacturer does not recommend breastfeeding during treatment. Infants exposed to antipsychotics via milk have been reported to have sedation, irritability, poor feeding, motor abnormalities, and slowed development. If exposure occurs, monitor the infant closely—especially if premature or low birth weight, or if the parent is taking other sedating medications.
special_populations.pediatric: For psychiatric and psychotic disorders, children’s doses are based on weight and need specialist care. The injection should not be used in children under 1 year because of safety concerns. Children and teens may be more sensitive to movement side effects and sleepiness, so the dose is raised carefully with close monitoring.
special_populations.geriatric: Best avoided for behavior problems linked to dementia or delirium unless non-drug approaches have failed and the person is at risk of harming themselves or others. Even when it is appropriate (for example, schizophrenia or bipolar disorder), older adults are more sensitive to sleepiness and to dizziness or fainting when standing up (a drop in blood pressure). The lowest dose that works is used, raised slowly and reviewed often, with attempts to reduce or stop it once things are stable.
special_populations.renal_impairment: There is no formal dose change; it is used with caution. If you have kidney problems, the injection is best avoided when possible.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: It should not be used if you have liver problems.

pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Oral dosing is typically given with meals to reduce GI upset and improve tolerability.

dosing.titration: Dosing is highly symptom-driven: lower doses may be enough when the goal is anxiety relief or sleep, while mania/psychosis often require higher divided doses. If sedation is strong, clinicians often use smaller doses during the day and a higher dose at night. If injections are used, people are switched to tablets as soon as possible.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: For chronic psychiatric treatment, switching antipsychotics is often safer than abruptly stopping. If discontinuation is chosen (and it’s not an emergency due to a serious adverse reaction), taper gradually over weeks to months to watch for relapse and reduce withdrawal symptoms.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Methotrimeprazine (Nozinan) is a sedating, first-generation antipsychotic used in Canada for psychosis and bipolar disorder. In psychiatry, it’s most relevant when you need both antipsychotic effects and a strong calming/sedating effect—like severe agitation, insomnia tied to mania/psychosis, or short-term crisis-level anxiety.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders}: Helps reduce hallucinations, delusions, and agitation over days to weeks
{link:condition:bipolar-disorder:Bipolar disorder / acute mania}: Calms racing thoughts, agitation, and insomnia; mood stabilization improves over 1-2 weeks
{link:condition:generalized-anxiety-disorder:Severe anxiety (tablet-only labeling in Canada)}: Sometimes used short-term when sedation is a benefit
{link:condition:insomnia:Insomnia (short-term)}: A sedating option when non-med approaches haven’t worked and the benefits clearly outweigh risks
off_label: Acute agitation (especially when insomnia and agitation are driving the crisis)
Sedation support in palliative settings when distress and agitation are prominent
Short-term sleep rescue when insomnia is wrapped around mania/psychosis

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: It took the edge off the panic and the spinning thoughts.
I felt less revved up—like my nervous system got a seatbelt.
It felt like someone pulled the plug on my anxiety.
I was calm… but also kind of glued to the couch.
items.note: If sedation is too intense, clinicians often shift more of the dose to nighttime and keep daytime doses smaller.

quotes: Standing up made me feel woozy for a minute.
I had that ‘black spots’ moment when I got up too fast.
I had to slow down and hydrate or I’d feel faint.
items.note: Orthostatic hypotension (blood pressure drop when standing) is a real risk, especially with injections or higher doses.

items.category: Anticholinergic Stuff (dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision)
quotes: Dry mouth like I licked a desert.
Constipation was no joke—had to actually plan for it.
My eyes felt weird and my vision got a little blurry.

items.category: Movement Side Effects (EPS) in some people
quotes: Restless legs but like… my whole body wanted to crawl out of itself.
My muscles felt tight and awkward.
I got this stiff, shaky feeling that wasn’t me.
items.note: EPS can include restlessness (akathisia), stiffness, tremor, dystonia, and—over time—tardive dyskinesia.

sections.intro: This med has a vibe. It’s not subtle. When it works, people often describe a heavy calm that can be relieving—unless it tips into “I can’t function.”

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Methotrimeprazine can calm and sedate relatively quickly, but antipsychotic and antimanic benefits take longer. Timing also depends on route (oral vs injection) and what symptom you’re targeting.
key_points: IM: peak levels around 0.5-1.5 hours; calming effects for anxiety/tension may be felt around ~1 hour
Oral: peak levels around 1-3 hours; sedation may be noticeable the same day
Acute mania: some improvement may show up within days, with continued improvement over 1-2 weeks
Schizophrenia/psychosis: initial improvements may appear in 1-2 weeks, with fuller response over 4-6 weeks
Half-life ~15-30 hours: the drug can linger in the system even if the “strongest” felt effects come and go

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: This is a heavy-sedation antipsychotic. In real-world use, it’s often effective for dialing down agitation, helping with sleep, and taking the “threat level” out of severe anxiety. For mania and psychosis, expect a slower arc: early improvements can happen within the first week, but meaningful stabilization usually builds over 1-2 weeks (mania) and 4-6 weeks (psychosis).
sections.value: Often strong sedation + calming within hours; symptom improvement in mania/psychosis over days to weeks
sections.clinical_details: Methotrimeprazine is most useful when sedation is clinically helpful—like acute agitation, severe insomnia tied to mania/psychosis, or crisis-level anxiety—while still providing dopamine-blocking antipsychotic effects. The tradeoff is tolerability: orthostatic hypotension, anticholinergic effects, and movement risks can limit dosing and long-term use.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: This medication can cause severe sedation and dangerous drops in blood pressure. Avoid combining with alcohol, opioids, or other strong sedatives.
sections.black_box: Canadian boxed warning: Older adults with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death compared with placebo. Methotrimeprazine is not indicated for dementia-related psychosis in elderly patients.
other: Contraindicated in hepatic disease (liver disease is a hard stop).
QT prolongation and life-threatening arrhythmias have been reported with phenothiazines; risk rises with electrolyte problems and other QT-prolonging meds.
Orthostatic hypotension can be significant, especially after parenteral dosing or higher oral doses.
CNS depression: can impair driving, decision-making, coordination, and increase fall risk.
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and tardive dyskinesia can occur; risk increases with higher doses and longer exposure.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is rare but life-threatening: fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability.
Blood dyscrasias (like agranulocytosis) have been reported with antipsychotics: take infection symptoms seriously.
Anticholinergic effects can be intense: constipation, urinary retention, blurry vision, dry mouth; paralytic ileus is an emergency.
Temperature regulation problems: higher risk with heat exposure, dehydration, strenuous exercise, and other anticholinergic meds.
patient_counseling: If you feel faint when standing, sit back down, hydrate, and tell your prescriber—don’t try to power through it.
No alcohol. Avoid opioids and other sedatives unless your prescriber explicitly coordinates it.
Don’t drive until you know exactly how sedating this is for you.
Call urgently for fever + stiffness + confusion, or severe muscle rigidity (possible NMS).
Report new restlessness, muscle stiffness, tremor, jaw/neck tightness, or abnormal movements early—these are treatable if caught quickly.
Treat constipation like a real side effect, not an afterthought (hydration, fiber, stool softener plan if needed).
If you’re older, have heart issues, or have a history of falls, this med needs extra caution and slower dosing.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common issues are heavy sedation, dizziness/orthostatic hypotension, anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention), and movement side effects (EPS).
plain_language_list: Weight gain and metabolic changes in some people
Sex hormone side effects from prolactin changes (period changes, libido changes, breast changes)

common.patient_note: This is a sedating antipsychotic. Many people feel sleepy, slowed, or “heavy,” especially early on or after dose increases. If daytime sedation is too much, clinicians often shift more dosing to bedtime and keep daytime doses smaller.
This can happen even at therapeutic doses and is more likely with injections and higher doses. Get up slowly, hydrate, and let your prescriber know if you’re having near-fainting episodes.

common.symptom: Anticholinergic Effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurry vision)
common.patient_note: Dry mouth and constipation are common with phenothiazines. Constipation can become severe—don’t ignore it. Urinary retention or severe belly pain needs urgent evaluation.
EPS can look like inner restlessness (akathisia), stiffness, tremor, slowed movement, or muscle spasms. Tell your prescriber quickly—early management matters.
Glucose intolerance and hyperglycemia have been reported with antipsychotics. If you have diabetes or are at risk, monitoring matters.
Antipsychotics can raise prolactin. Symptoms can include menstrual changes, low libido, erectile/ejaculatory changes, breast tenderness, or galactorrhea.

Serious arrhythmias/QT prolongation/torsades de pointes: fainting, palpitations, sudden collapse. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Severe hypotension/circulatory collapse (especially parenteral): syncope, shock. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.

sections.intro: Big picture: this medication stacks sedation and blood-pressure-lowering effects with other meds. Also watch QT risk and anticholinergic burden.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: For chronic psychiatric treatment, switching antipsychotics is often safer than abruptly stopping. If discontinuation is chosen (and it’s not an emergency due to a serious adverse reaction), taper gradually over weeks to months to watch for relapse and reduce withdrawal symptoms.
key_points: If you stop suddenly—especially from higher doses—you can get withdrawal symptoms: agitation, anxiety, sweating, insomnia, GI upset (nausea/vomiting), tremor, dizziness/vertigo, restlessness, muscle aches, odd temperature sensations, runny nose, dyskinesias, and rebound psychosis.
Relapse risk matters: people with chronic symptoms, repeated relapses, and clear schizophrenia features are at higher risk for poor outcomes with abrupt discontinuation.

Common switching strategies: cross-titration (gradually decrease the first while increasing the new), overlap (keep the old at full dose while the new is raised, then taper the old over 1-2 weeks), or abrupt change (less preferred for high-relapse-risk patients).
If side effects are intolerable, don’t white-knuckle it—tell your prescriber. Dose adjustments or switching can often solve the problem without destabilizing you.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Dosing is highly symptom-driven: lower doses may be enough when the goal is anxiety relief or sleep, while mania/psychosis often require higher divided doses. If sedation is strong, clinicians often use smaller doses during the day and a higher dose at night. If injections are used, people are switched to tablets as soon as possible.

adult.anxiety_initial: 6-25 mg/day PO in 3 divided doses with meals
adult.anxiety_titration: Increase gradually based on response and tolerability
adult.bipolar_or_mania_oral_titration: Increase based on response and tolerability; if starting 100-200 mg/day, remain in bed for the first few days due to hypotension/sedation risk
adult.psychosis_oral_titration: Increase based on response and tolerability; if starting at 100-200 mg/day, stay in bed for the first few days; very high doses (≥1 g/day) may be needed for some people with psychosis under specialist oversight
adult.acute_agitation_im: 25 mg IM 3-4 times daily (switch to oral as soon as possible)
adult.sleep_prn: 10-25 mg PO as a single bedtime dose (short-term use; generally avoid long-term use beyond 4 weeks unless nonpharmacologic options are not available/effective and benefits outweigh risks)
adult.insomnia_im: 25 mg IM as a single bedtime dose (when IM is clinically necessary; switch to oral ASAP)
adult.renal_impairment: No manufacturer-provided dose adjustment; use with caution. Avoid parenteral use in renal impairment when possible.

sections.simple_explanation: Lower doses can be used when the goal is sedation for sleep or short-term anxiety relief. Higher divided doses are used for mania and psychosis. Because it can cause significant sleepiness and blood pressure drops, dosing often gets “shifted” toward nighttime if daytime functioning is getting wrecked.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Use in pregnancy and breastfeeding requires careful risk-benefit decisions. Older adults are more vulnerable to confusion, falls, and low blood pressure—especially in dementia or delirium, where antipsychotics carry increased mortality risk.
sections.pregnancy: Data on methotrimeprazine specifically are limited. As a class, first-generation antipsychotics have not shown a clear major malformation signal overall, but late-pregnancy exposure to antipsychotics can cause newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, abnormal muscle tone, tremor, feeding problems, respiratory distress, somnolence). Tapering late in pregnancy to prevent newborn symptoms is generally not recommended; instead, use the lowest effective dose and avoid polypharmacy when possible. For anxiety in pregnancy, other options are usually preferred.
sections.lactation: Present in human milk; the manufacturer does not recommend breastfeeding during treatment. Infants exposed to antipsychotics via milk have been reported to have sedation, irritability, poor feeding, motor abnormalities, and slowed development. If exposure occurs, monitor the infant closely—especially if premature or low birth weight, or if the parent is taking other sedating medications.
sections.pediatrics: For psychiatric/psychotic disorders and related indications, pediatric dosing is weight-based and requires specialist management. Parenteral use is contraindicated in children <1 year due to safety concerns. Children/adolescents may be more vulnerable to movement side effects and sedation; titrate carefully and monitor closely.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid for behavioral problems associated with dementia or delirium unless non-drug approaches have failed and the person is at risk of harming themselves or others. Even when appropriate (e.g., schizophrenia or bipolar disorder), older adults are more sensitive to sedation and orthostatic hypotension (dizziness or fainting when standing). Use the lowest effective dose, titrate slowly, reassess often, and consider attempts to reduce or stop it when stable.
sections.renal: No formal dose adjustment provided; use with caution. Avoid parenteral use in renal impairment when possible.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mental status and alertness every visit: sedation level, confusion, and whether daytime functioning is getting crushed.
Blood pressure and orthostatics, especially after starting, after dose increases, and after parenteral doses; watch for dizziness/falls.
EPS monitoring at every visit (akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism). Use a formal rating scale at least annually, or every 6 months if high risk.
Tardive dyskinesia monitoring at every visit and with a formal scale at least annually (more often if high risk).
Fall risk assessment as clinically indicated; extra vigilance in older adults and those with prior falls.

Metabolic monitoring: weight/BMI frequently early (every visit for first months, then periodically), fasting glucose/HbA1c and lipids at baseline and periodically (e.g., around 4 months after initiation and annually, sooner if abnormal).
CBC as clinically indicated, especially if infection symptoms occur (fever, sore throat) or if history of low WBC/drug-induced neutropenia.
Electrolytes and renal function as clinically indicated; monitor sodium in older adults (hyponatremia/SIADH risk).
ECG when clinically indicated (history of QT issues, cardiac disease, syncope, multiple QT-prolonging meds, electrolyte risk).
Prolactin symptom screening: ask about menstrual changes, libido changes, gynecomastia, galactorrhea, erectile/ejaculatory issues; check prolactin if symptomatic.
Constipation and urinary retention checks: treat constipation early; urgent evaluation for severe abdominal pain/distention or inability to urinate.
Temperature regulation: counsel on heat exposure, dehydration, and strenuous exercise—especially with anticholinergic co-meds.
Ocular symptoms: assess vision changes; consider eye exam if prolonged exposure or symptoms arise.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Availability is Canada-focused. Formulations may vary by product. In psychiatry, oral dosing is preferred when possible; injections are typically used short-term, and people are switched to tablets as soon as practical.
items: Oral tablets (Canada/generics): 2 mg, 5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg
Injection solution (Canada): Nozinan 25 mg/mL (1 mL) (contains sodium sulfite)
Not available in the United States

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Methotrimeprazine is an aliphatic phenothiazine that blocks dopamine receptors (D1/D2), which helps reduce psychosis and manic activation over time. It also hits alpha receptors, serotonin receptors, and muscarinic receptors—this is a big reason it’s so sedating and why it can cause low blood pressure, dry mouth, constipation, and blurry vision.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In modern psychiatry, this isn’t usually a first-choice long-term antipsychotic because the side effect load can be heavy (sedation, hypotension, anticholinergic burden, EPS/TD risk). Where it can make sense is when sedation is clinically useful—severe agitation, insomnia tied to mania/psychosis, or short-term stabilization—especially in settings where this medication is commonly available (Canada) and when alternatives aren’t tolerated or effective.

faqs.q: What is methotrimeprazine (Nozinan) used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In psychiatry, it’s used for schizophrenia/psychosis and bipolar disorder (including acute mania). It’s also sometimes used short-term for severe anxiety or insomnia when sedation is actually helpful. It’s not available in the United States, but it is used in Canada.

faqs.q: Is Nozinan basically a sleeping pill?
faqs.a: It can feel like one because it’s very sedating, but it’s actually an antipsychotic. The sleep effect is a side effect that can be used on purpose in certain situations (like mania with insomnia or severe agitation). It’s not meant to be a long-term insomnia medication.

Sedation and calming can show up within hours (and injections can feel faster). For mania, early improvements may be noticed within days, with continued improvements over 1 to 2 weeks. For psychosis, initial effects may appear in 1 to 2 weeks, with fuller response building over 4 to 6 weeks.

faqs.q: What’s the biggest side effect people notice?
faqs.a: Sedation and dizziness when standing (low blood pressure). Dry mouth and constipation are also common. Some people develop movement side effects like restlessness (akathisia), stiffness, or tremor.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on this medication?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol plus a sedating antipsychotic is a bad combo: more sedation, worse coordination and judgment, higher fall risk, and potentially dangerous CNS/respiratory depression—especially if other sedatives are also involved.

faqs.q: Is it safe for older adults or dementia?
faqs.a: It needs extra caution in older adults because of sleepiness, dizziness or fainting when standing up (a drop in blood pressure), confusion, and fall risk. There is also a Canadian boxed warning: older adults with dementia-related psychosis who take antipsychotics have a higher risk of death than those taking a placebo. It is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.

faqs.q: What are EPS and tardive dyskinesia (TD), and should I worry?
faqs.a: EPS are movement side effects (restlessness, stiffness, tremor, muscle spasms). Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is a condition of involuntary movements, often of the face or mouth, that can last and can develop with longer-term use. Older antipsychotics carry this risk, so regular checks and telling your prescriber early about any new movements matter.

faqs.q: Does it affect the heart rhythm (QT)?
faqs.a: It can. Phenothiazines have been associated with changes in cardiac conduction and QT prolongation, and serious arrhythmias have been reported. Risk increases if you’re on other QT-prolonging meds or have low potassium/magnesium, heart disease, or fainting episodes.

Tablets are usually taken with meals. If sleepiness is too strong during the day, prescribers often use smaller daytime doses and a larger bedtime dose. If injections are used, people are usually switched to tablets as soon as possible, and lying down after an injection is often recommended to lower the risk of a drop in blood pressure.

If it’s being used short-term at low doses, stopping may be straightforward—but if you’ve been on higher doses or longer-term, stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms and can also trigger relapse of mania or psychosis. When discontinuation is planned and not due to a serious adverse reaction, a gradual taper over weeks to months is usually safer.

Data for methotrimeprazine specifically are limited. Antipsychotic exposure in the third trimester can cause newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms. For breastfeeding, the manufacturer does not recommend use; the medication is present in human milk and infant sedation/feeding problems are concerns. Decisions should be individualized with shared decision-making.

seo.description: Nozinan (methotrimeprazine/levomepromazine) is a very sedating typical antipsychotic used in Canada for psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe anxiety, and short-term insomnia. Learn dosing, onset, side effects (low blood pressure, EPS), interactions, and how to taper safely.
